planting.note: Attach a young plant to a rough bark slab or moss pole with the leaf undersides facing the support; keep the surface consistently moist so the stem roots can grip and the shingling habit develops.

directions: Grow Monstera dubia pressed against a vertical bark slab, tree trunk, or moss pole in bright, indirect light with high humidity, since the juvenile plant only develops its distinctive flattened, overlapping leaf pattern when climbing a rough textured surface. Native from Mexico south through the Amazon basin, this slow-growing epiphytic aroid produces small, dark green, silver-patterned leaves that lie almost completely flat against its support like roof shingles while young. Given years of upward growth and enough height on its support, older stems can eventually shift to larger, more typically shaped Monstera foliage, though this transition is rarely seen in home cultivation. Keep soil evenly moist but not soggy and avoid cold drafts, as this species has no frost tolerance.

planting.note: Set against a rough-barked tree, rock wall, or bark totem in deep shade; mist regularly while the stem roots establish contact with the support surface.

directions: Rhaphidophora hayi is a lithophytic and epiphytic climber from the rainforests of tropical Queensland, Australia, that presses its small, overlapping juvenile leaves flat against rock faces and tree trunks in a shingling growth habit similar to its more widely grown relatives. Provide a rough, damp-friable surface such as cork bark or a lava rock slab so the flattened stem can adhere and root along its length, and keep humidity consistently high. Mature, higher-climbing growth produces larger, more conventionally shaped leaves, but plants are almost always grown and sold in their compact juvenile form. Protect from any temperature below the mid-50s Fahrenheit and keep out of direct sun, which scorches the thin juvenile foliage.

planting.note: Provide a sturdy, wide totem or trellis from the start since mature vines and their large leaves become heavy; keep in partial to deep shade with rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Native to the Indo-China and Malesian region including Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, and Peninsular Malaysia, Epipremnum giganteum is a large-growing climbing aroid whose thick, glossy, entire leaves stay unlobed and unperforated even at full maturity, distinguishing it from fenestrated relatives like Epipremnum pinnatum. Give it a substantial climbing support and generous space, since a well-grown specimen can eventually carry leaves well over a foot long on a heavy vining stem. It performs best in warm, humid, sheltered shade with consistently moist but free-draining soil, and it has no cold tolerance below the upper 40s Fahrenheit. This species is still uncommon outside specialist aroid collections, making it a distinctive addition to a Gulf Coast shade garden or large greenhouse planting.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide established clumps at the rhizome and replant in rich, humus-heavy soil in deep shade; keep consistently moist and warm while new roots establish.

directions: Native to Venezuela, Colombia, and Panama, this compact, rhizomatous understory aroid is grown for its glossy, arching, dark green leaves brushed with marbled yellow-gold markings. It forms a low, clumping mound well suited to deep shade beneath larger tropical foliage or as a groundcover in a sheltered courtyard bed in zones 9-11. Keep the soil rich in organic matter and evenly moist, since this species is intolerant of both drought and waterlogged conditions, and protect it from any temperature drop near freezing. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to refresh vigor and produce new starts.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in loose, humus-rich soil in a shaded, humid spot such as a shade house, terrarium, or sheltered garden bed; avoid letting the soil dry out.

directions: Found on rainforest floors in tropical Asia and South America, Homalomena picturata is a clumping aroid prized for its deep green, heart-shaped to oblong leaves marked with a paler, painterly white stripe radiating along the prominent midvein. It stays low and dense, making it a good choice for the front of a shaded tropical border, a shade-house pot, or a humid terrarium in climates outside its hardiness range. Grow it in constantly warm, humid, deeply shaded conditions with rich, evenly moist soil, since exposure to direct sun or dry air quickly dulls and browns the leaf edges. Established clumps can be divided in spring to produce additional plants.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or offsets in rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to deep shade; wear gloves when handling, since the sap is irritating to skin.

directions: Alocasia denudata is an upright, smooth-stemmed elephant ear native to the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and Borneo, where it grows in shaded lowland forest and is traditionally known locally as a source of intensely irritating sap once used to treat skin ailments or as a fish poison. In the garden it forms a tall clump of glossy, arrow-shaped mid-green leaves on slender, often mottled petioles, giving it a more refined, upright silhouette than bulkier Alocasia species. Grow it in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, and keep it away from areas where children or pets might handle the foliage. Caution: the sap contains calcium oxalate raphides and causes significant skin and mucous membrane irritation on contact or if ingested.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
